newsitem.title: USA: Compaq cuts prices of desktop computers for business.
newsitem.headline: Compaq cuts prices of desktop computers for business.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp. Thursday said it was cutting prices on desktop computers for corporate users and changing its distribution strategy, in a move to better compete with direct marketer Dell Computer Corp.
The announcement came a day after Hewlett-Packard Co. said it would cut prices on many corporate personal computers up to 24 percent, in what could lead to a price war among PC makers.

Compaq also said its earnings fell 20 percent in the second quarter due to a one-time charge related to an acquisition, but its results excluding the charge were about in line with expectations on Wall Street.

Industry analysts said the price moves by Compaq and Hewlett-Packard were meant to compete with Dell, which ships products directly to customers without using distributors and retailers and thus can offer lower prices.
Dell is by far the fastest growing of the major PC makers.
The changes by Compaq could ripple through the industry the way its big price cuts did five years ago, changing the competitive landscape, the analysts said.

"Without taking some form of action to meet the competition from Dell and, to a lesser extent, the other direct vendors like Gateway (2000 Inc.) there would be no stopping Dell," analyst Eugene Glazer at Fortis Advisers said ahead of Compaq's announcement.
"Dell is far more efficient, their inventory risk is much lower and they can get new technology to the market faster."

Compaq said it cut prices up to 22 percent on corporate desktop computers and introduced 13 new machines starting at $1,199. The company also said it expects to be making all its products to order by year-end.
Dell, Gateway and other direct marketers take orders over the telephone or the Internet from consumers and companies for machines built to order.

Compaq and Hewlett-Packard hope that if they lower prices enough, companies building networks of desktop machines will order from them because of their reputation for service, rather than deal with the direct marketers.

Compaq said its new Deskpro 2000 line starts at $1,199 to $1,899 and Deskpro 4000 models range from $1,389 to $2,089. It also cut prices on older machines. For example, a Deskpro 2000 PC with an Intel 166 MHz Pentium chip will now be $999, a cut of 16 percent, the company said.
Compaq, which is based in Houston, said second-quarter profits fell 20 percent as it took a $208 million charge related to its acquisition of Microcom Inc.

The company said net income fell to $214 million, or 75 cents a share, in the quarter, from $267 million, or 97 cents a share, a year earlier. Sales, however, jumped 25 percent to $5 billion from $4 billion.

Compaq said the $208 million charge it took to write off technology in the Microcom deal knocked 73 cents off its earnings per share. Without the charge, net income would have been $422 million, or $1.48 a share, for the quarter.
Wall Street had been expecting the company to post income of $1.39 a share, according to First Call, which tracks analysts' estimates.
Compaq acquired Microcom, a maker of modems and other technology based in Norwood, Mass., for $280 million in April.
Compaq's stock fell $2.50 to $118.50 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange. It had risen almost $24 in the past 10 session as traders bet on strong results.
